water.quote: The Bubble tip anemone (Entacmaea quadricolor) is very popular in the saltwater aquarium hobby.

sections.html:
The Bubble tip anemone (Entacmaea quadricolor) is very popular in the saltwater aquarium hobby. It is prized for its beautiful form, colours and the bulbous swellings at the tips of its tentacles. Although fairly hardy, it is intolerant of large variations in water chemistry, so it suits stable, established reef tanks.

  • Minimum tank: 120 litres
  • Keeping: moderate; propagation: moderate
  • Lighting: medium to high; water flow: moderate
  • Salinity: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: up to 10 ppm
  • Feeding: photosynthetic, needs supplemental food
  • Size: up to 30 cm and more
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Toxic: yes; invasive: no; temper: aggressive
  • Colour forms: red/rose, orange, green, brown and pink

Bubble tip anemone is well known in the reef hobby, so many local fish stores and online retailers carry it. The price varies with size, rarity and colour; for example, green and rose Bubble tip anemones cost less than the black widow type, and both are highly sought after.

Choose healthy specimens: a robust body and attachment to solid substrate or the glass are good signs. Avoid large specimens, since they do not ship as well as small or medium ones. Healthy specimens can be difficult to separate from live rock; if so, take the rock together with the anemone.

Aquacultured (captive-bred) specimens are recommended over wild-caught ones, as they are hardier and settle into aquarium conditions more easily.

This species is an excellent choice for experienced hobbyists who enjoy diversity in their reef tanks.

Bubble tip anemone is a species of sea anemone in the family Actiniidae. It is commonly found in the tropical waters of the Indo-Pacific, including the Red Sea. Entacmaea quadricolor occurs throughout the tropical waters of the Indian Ocean, Red Sea, Fiji, Indonesia, Tonga and the Philippines.

Classification: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Cnidaria, Class Anthozoa, Order Actinaria, Family Actiniidae, Genus Entacmaea.

Bubble tip anemones can be found even in deeper water (up to 60 m) with dim light, where they are generally attached to coral rubble or in crevices of solid reefs. This is usually seen in large adults with longer, thinner tentacles, whereas smaller, younger specimens live in groups or colonies (sometimes solitary) closer to the surface and enjoy bright light.
Due to its growth potential and its ability to reproduce easily, it should be housed in a tank of at least 120 litres.

Bubble tip anemone is moderately difficult to care for. It tends to anchor firmly in crevices, and trying to move it may tear the flesh, causing severe injury or even death. Removing it is easy to do damage; use something dull, such as an old credit card, put it under the foot and lift gently. Do not touch it with bare hands: the stings can cause a skin rash for a few days.

It can be hard to keep with other corals because it can sting them. Even with ample spacing to prevent chemical warfare, it can move back; if it anchors close to corals, you have to move them elsewhere. Some aquarists even use torch corals to keep Bubble tip anemones at bay.

Long tentacles are a sign that it needs more food and/or light with less flow.

Because of its roaming behaviour, monitor it closely and cover filter intakes enough to prevent it from being sucked into pumps.

Placement: it hardly matters where you put it, since like all anemones it can move around the tank. There is no definite pattern: one day it may roam, or it may stay still for weeks, and it does not seem to be searching for a better place.

Common problems

  • Extensive growth: under optimal conditions it is prolific, and several new anemones may appear in a short time, overpopulating a small tank and bothering fish and corals.
  • Splitting: if it keeps splitting, it may be a sign of stress (mostly poor water quality, sudden temperature change or too large water changes). Some aquarists use this deliberately to induce splitting.
  • Roaming: while roaming it may sting assumed prey or nearby corals, and may wander into a filter or pump intake.
  • Bleaching: high temperatures induce bleaching. A study found that anemonefish facilitated bleaching recovery in a host sea anemone, enhancing its resilience.
  • After-death effect: when a Bubble tip anemone dies, it can kill the entire system. Keep this in mind if you propagate by cutting in two.

• Temperature: 22–28°C
  • pH: 8.1–8.4
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH
  • Specific gravity: 1.023–1.025
  • Calcium: 374–425 ppm
  • Magnesium: 1,200–1,300 ppm
  • Strontium: 8–10 ppm
  • Nitrate: below 10 ppm
  • Phosphate: below 0.03 ppm
  • Ammonia: 0 ppm

Bubble tip anemones cannot handle major changes in water parameters well, so keep conditions as stable as possible. Avoid changing a very large percentage of water at once; replace about 5% weekly, 10% every two weeks and 20% monthly to maintain good water quality and replenish depleted nutrients.

Lighting: the anemone benefits from the photosynthetic activity of the algae living in its tissue, so provide ample light. Moderate to high light works best, but it should not be excessive, to prevent bleaching. Bubble tip anemones thrive under VHO, T5 and LED lighting.

Flow: maintain moderate water movement, just enough to carry suspended food to the tentacles and remove debris and waste from its body. Avoid placing the anemone where it is hit by direct flow. Some aquarists claim that under slight flow the anemone stays in bubble form.

Cover filter and pump intakes enough to prevent the anemone from being sucked in.

Nutrition from photosynthesis is often enough to sustain the anemone for long periods, and it can also extend its tentacles to capture food in the water column. Even so, manual supplemental feeding keeps it healthy.

Feed finely chopped shrimp, mussels, clam, krill and fish. Simply place the food on the tentacles, two or three times a week. Do not overfeed: use a small serving each time to avoid leftovers and waste in the reef tank. If it spits out the food, you are overfeeding.

  • Photosynthetic: yes
  • Diet type: carnivore
  • Feeding frequency: 2–3 times a week

The anemones are semi-aggressive. They have sweeper tentacles with stinging cells (cnidocytes) that can immobilise or kill prey on impact. They tend to stay attached to solid substrates with the base in crevices, but may also roam open areas or attach to the aquarium walls. It is one of the few anemones that can host clownfish without any issues.

Many clownfish species coexist with Bubble tip anemones in the wild, and this can be replicated in an aquarium. Common examples:

  • Maroon clownfish (Premnas biaculeatus)
  • Tomato clownfish (Amphiprion frenatus)
  • Fire clownfish or red saddleback clownfish (Amphiprion ephippium)
  • Cinnamon clownfish (Amphiprion melanopus)
  • Clark's clownfish (Amphiprion clarkii)
  • Allard's clownfish (Amphiprion allardi)
  • Two-band clownfish (Amphiprion bicintus)
  • McCulloch's clownfish (Amphiprion mccullochi)
  • Three-band clownfish (Amphiprion tricintus)

Anemonefish influence oxygen levels of the host anemone by altering flow around its tissues, which increases oxygen availability and absorption and thereby raises metabolic rates.

Bubble tip anemone reproduces in several ways.

  • In nature it mainly reproduces sexually: males and females release sperm and eggs (gametes) into the water, which you will notice as cloudiness in the tank. Fertilised eggs develop into larvae, but the larvae do not survive in an aquarium. According to some studies they can remain in the plankton for up to 2 months before settling, so do not rely on this way of getting new anemones.
  • An adult can split into two, creating a new anemone.
  • In saltwater tanks you may frag (cut) a grown anemone to form a new individual. This can easily kill it if something goes wrong, so it is not recommended. If you still want to, use a scalpel or sharp razor blade and cut the specimen lengthwise, then place the halves in the tank, preferably in areas with moderate flow and lighting.

The name "bubble tip" comes from the bulbous tips at the ends of the tentacles. In some specimens the bubble tips are absent, giving longer, thinner tentacles. What causes this is still unclear. Theories include: not enough protein in the diet; too much food (it relies mostly on light, so fed anemones no longer need bubbles); not enough algae in the water; not enough nitrate; too much flow; bubbles kept when disturbed or stressed, or when relaxed; or bubbles adding surface area to compensate for lower light and photosynthesis. Some of these theories contradict each other. The anemone may also lose its bubble tips after a long spell of poor lighting and poor water quality.

Bubble tip anemones can grow up to 30 cm or more in diameter and come in colour morphs including red/rose, orange, green, brown and pink. The red or rose form is the most common, attractive, prolific and inexpensive. The blood red form (black widow anemone), green, brown, pink and orange variants are also sold.
